title: His face shone (Luke 9:28–36)
hook: he was praying when his face changed; Moses and Elijah talk of his departure

segments.voice: Yesterday, Peter's answer and the daily cross. Your line was daily. Did you pick up your ordinary weight on purpose this morning? Day five hundred thirty-six.

About eight days after the talk of the cross, Jesus takes three friends, Peter, John and James, and climbs a mountain. Luke tells us why: they went up "to pray." Some people describe a place, a hospital chapel, a hilltop, a kitchen at 4am, where they sat in prayer or silence long enough that something in the room seemed to change. Not dramatically. Just a shift. The three disciples are tired. Luke says they were "heavy with sleep." And while they're fighting to keep their eyes open, Jesus keeps praying. And then his face begins to change.

In the King James words: "And as he prayed, the fashion of his countenance was altered, and his raiment was white and glistering." As he prayed. That's Luke's own emphasis. Matthew says his face did shine as the sun; Luke says it changed while he was praying. The light comes in the middle of prayer. Then two men are talking with him, Moses and Elijah, the lawgiver and the prophet. In Exodus, Moses' own face shone after he spoke with God on a mountain. And what are they talking about? Luke tells us: they "spake of his decease which he should accomplish at Jerusalem." Decease, in Greek, is exodos: a departure, a way out. Some readers hear in it the book of Exodus, the story of Moses leading Israel out of slavery. Here, standing next to Moses, Jesus talks about his own exodus, the death and rising waiting for him in Jerusalem. Peter wakes up enough to say something, anything: "Master, it is good for us to be here: and let us make three tabernacles." Three shelters, three tents. Stay, make it last. Luke adds kindly that he didn't know what he was saying. Then a cloud covers them, and a voice: "This is my beloved Son: hear him." When the cloud lifts, Jesus is alone. And they tell no one in those days. Churches remember this as the Transfiguration, the change of form. But in Luke, the change doesn't come from nowhere. It comes while he prays.
screen: then, large: `AS HE PRAYED, THE FASHION OF HIS COUNTENANCE WAS ALTERED.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: stay in the quiet until something shifts. Settle, and breathe. Don't aim for a vision. Aim for staying. Close your eyes and let yourself sit past the point where you'd normally stop. The first minute is often noisy: lists, worries, tiredness, like the disciples heavy with sleep. Keep going. Breathe. Notice the moment, if it comes, when something softens. A thought loosens. Your shoulders drop. The noise thins. It might be very small. Don't grab at it, the way Peter wanted to build shelters. Just notice it. If you pray, you can let the words run out and simply stay. If you don't, simply stay. The bell holds the time.
His face shone. On a mountain, while Jesus prays, his face changes and his clothes blaze white, and Moses and Elijah speak with him about his exodus.
Your line: while he prayed. Today, find one quiet stretch and stay in it a little longer than feels natural. Notice what shifts. Day five hundred thirty-six.

howItsDone: Churches in several traditions keep a feast of the Transfiguration, and some Protestant churches mark Transfiguration Sunday just before Lent.

original.note: Greek: a going out, departure. the "decease" of Luke 9:31, and the name of the book of Exodus.

trapdoor: what you thought: Jesus glowed on a mountain.
what it means: in Luke, the change comes while he prays, and Moses and Elijah talk with him about what waits in Jerusalem.
what a scholar hears: his "decease" is exodos, and some scholars hear in it a new exodus, spoken of beside Moses.

notes: The index title 'His face shone' echoes Matthew 17:2; Luke says his countenance 'was altered'. The script notes the difference.
'Only Luke' says they went up to pray and that the change came as he prayed; Mark and Matthew do not mention prayer. Confirm.
Exodos (9:31) and its link to the Exodus: widely noted.
Transfiguration feast dates by tradition (August 6; Transfiguration Sunday in many Protestant lectionaries). Confirm.

Editor review (2026-10-01): cut 'only Luke' (twice, plus its myth item), 'the greatest of the prophets' for Elijah, 'centuries earlier', the invented 'long climb', and the question that assumed the listener prays; 'kept quiet for a long time' corrected to 9:36's 'in those days'; the exodus reading attributed to readers/scholars; feast-date claim generalized.
